prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: From, When, Stop

outputs.L1:
From the old bridge where we’d been stopped, it looked, a little below us, like a diving board. When the girl switched her sign from Stop to Slow, I saw, across the river, three men standing at its base like old-fashioned divers—the men in swim caps we’d seen in newsreels.

“Hard hats,” you said, literal you.

You agreed it was “like a diving board,” but with no spring to it. Something below was holding it up, something concrete. It was the business of your life. Concrete—but to me, the men were waiting their turn over there, each competing for the best two-and-a-half gainer with which to knife the Tye River.

“They’d die,” you said.

“That’s a fine span,” I learned. “A very long one—they didn’t make ’em like that back then.”

Or us either, I thought, as I almost saw the hard hat bounce at the tip, one knee raised to his waist.

“Inspectors,” you said as we drove across. “Lollygagging.”

Whichever. Our span is ready.
outputs.L2:
From the aging bridge where traffic had halted, the structure just downstream resembled a platform for diving. Once the flagger turned her paddle from STOP to SLOW, I noticed three men on the opposite bank, gathered at the end of the span like the vintage swimmers in bathing caps we had watched in newsreels.

“They’re wearing hard hats,” you corrected, always insisting on exactness.

You accepted the diving-board comparison, though you pointed out that the bridge had no bounce. A concrete support underneath kept it aloft. Concrete was your life’s work. Yet I imagined the men lined up, each hoping to perform the finest two-and-a-half gainer before slicing into the Tye River.

They would be killed, you told me.

You taught me to call it an impressive span—an unusually long one, especially since bridges were not built that way in those days. Neither were we, I thought, while nearly picturing one of the hard-hatted men springing from the edge, a knee lifted level with his waist.

“Inspectors,” you said as we crossed. “Standing around wasting time.”

No matter. The distance between us is prepared.

As the description develops, however, the aging bridge takes on a deeper symbolic meaning. Its endurance, wear, and uncertain future reflect the relationship between the speaker and the companion. outputs.L4:
They stopped halfway across the old bridge, where the river widened and slowed beneath them. The bridge had not carried traffic for years. Weeds pushed through cracks in the asphalt, and rust spread across the railings in reddish scales. Downstream, a new concrete span was rising beside it, supported by pale columns that emerged from the water like unfinished monuments.

Daniel leaned against the railing and watched the workers below. One of them guided a suspended beam while another signaled to the crane operator with both arms.

“They’ll set that section before dark,” he said. “Once the beam is seated, they can pour the deck above it. The weight has to be distributed evenly across the piers.”

Mara followed his gaze. To her, the workers looked impossibly small against the machinery and the gray sweep of concrete.

“It looks as if they’re teaching the bridge how to reach the other side,” she said.

Daniel smiled. “The bridge isn’t reaching. It’s being assembled.”

“I know.”

“You always make things more mysterious than they are.”

“And you always make them less mysterious.”

The words were gentle, but they settled between them with more weight than either had intended.

A truck moved slowly along the construction road below, raising a cloud of dust. Beyond the new bridge lay the northern bank, where the town thinned into fields. Somewhere past those fields was the highway they would take if they left: first east toward the city, then north toward a life neither of them had seen except in photographs and property listings.

Daniel had already been offered the job. The contract was folded in the inside pocket of his jacket, though both of them knew every line of it by now. Better pay. A permanent position. A small apartment for the first six months. He had listed the facts so often that they had begun to sound like engineering specifications.

Mara had answered with possibilities. New streets. New windows. A room where she might paint again. The chance to become different people—or, as Daniel corrected her, the chance to live in a different place.

Still, they had not decided.

Daniel tapped the railing. A flake of rust fell away beneath his finger.

“This bridge was built in 1938,” he said. “It wasn’t designed for modern loads. Even if they repaired the surface, the structure would still be inadequate.”

Mara looked along the empty road behind them. “It carried everyone for almost a hundred years.”

“That doesn’t mean it can keep doing so.”

“No,” she said. “I suppose not.”

He turned toward her, hearing what she had not said. For months they had spoken about their life in the same indirect way, circling the question as if it were a hole in the floor. They had been together eleven years. They knew each other’s habits, silences, and small evasions. They knew how to survive ordinary disappointments. What they did not know was whether survival had become the only thing holding them together.

Below, the crane lowered the beam by inches. The workers pulled on guide ropes to keep it from turning in the wind.

“They have to trust one another,” Mara said.

“They have procedures.”

“That isn’t the opposite of trust.”

Daniel considered this. “No. I guess it isn’t.”

The beam descended toward the waiting supports. For a moment it hung above the gap, neither part of the bridge nor separate from it. Mara slipped her hand into Daniel’s. His fingers closed around hers automatically, then more firmly.

“I’m afraid we’ll go,” she said, “and discover that changing everything doesn’t change us.”

“I’m afraid we’ll stay,” he replied, “and spend the rest of our lives wondering why we didn’t go.”

It was the first time either of them had said the fear plainly.

On the new span, the workers shouted. The beam shifted, swung once, and settled into place. Even from a distance they could hear the deep metallic knock as it met its bearings.

Mara watched until the crane cables slackened.

“There,” she said. “It crossed.”

Daniel looked at the gap the beam had closed. “Not by itself.”

“No,” she agreed. “Not by itself.”

The sun had dropped behind the trees, and the old bridge’s shadow stretched across the river toward the new one. Daniel took the folded contract from his pocket. He did not open it. He simply held it between them.

“We could sign it tonight,” he said.

Mara studied his face. She saw the caution in it, the need for plans and measurements, but also something less certain and therefore more precious: a willingness to move before every risk had been calculated.

“Yes,” she said. “We could.”

They turned back toward the town, still holding hands. Behind them, the workers secured the newly placed beam as darkness gathered over the water. Ahead, the abandoned road led to the place where they had parked their car.

For now, they walked on the old bridge. But they no longer mistook it for the only way across.
outputs.L5:
**From, When, Stop**

From the moment we begin, we are always moving—toward a dream, away from a fear, or simply through another ordinary day.

When the road becomes difficult, we often believe that stopping means failure. But sometimes, we need to stop—not to surrender, but to breathe, look around, and remember why we started.

From every pause comes a new perspective. When we listen to ourselves, the next step becomes clearer.

Stop when you need to. Rest. Reflect. Then move forward again.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about a couple stopped at road construction on an old bridge, using the bridge as a metaphor for their strained relationship.
counterfactuals.output:
**One Lane Open**

We stop where the flagman lifts his palm,  
the old bridge narrowed  
to a single trembling lane.

Below us, the river keeps going—  
brown water shouldering branches,  
taking whatever falls.

Orange cones divide what remains.  
Men in bright vests bend over a wound  
opened in the asphalt,  
steel ribs showing through.

You turn down the radio.  
I watch your hands rest on the wheel  
as if waiting for instructions.

Once, we crossed without thinking,  
windows open,  
our laughter thrown into the trusses  
and returned to us  
made larger.

Now every beam is rusted at the joint.  
Every silence bears weight.

A sign says  
**EXPECT DELAYS**  
as though time alone  
were the trouble.

The flagman turns his sign—  
**SLOW**—  
and we move forward  
over patched plates  
that groan beneath us.

Neither of us speaks.

Halfway across,  
the river flashes through the gaps,  
and for one long second  
there is nothing under us  
but distance  
and the careful work  
of not falling.

On the other side,  
you reach for my hand.

Or perhaps only the gearshift.

Still, I leave my hand there,  
open between us,  
while behind our car  
the bridge holds,  
the workers lift their hammers,  
and the red light changes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a narrative poem in which the speaker imagines hard-hatted bridge inspectors as old-fashioned competitive divers while their practical companion keeps correcting them.
counterfactuals.output:
**Soundings**

We stopped where the river shouldered the town,  
brown-backed, muscling under the bridge.  
Above us, hard hats moved along the girders,  
yellow as caps in an old swim meet.

“Look,” I said, “the champions climb the high board—  
Varga of Hungary, poised for the swallow dive;  
Miller, the American, chalking his courage;  
the judge in white is lifting a card.”

“That’s a clipboard,” you said.  
“They’re checking rivets.  
And nobody’s diving.”

Still, one man edged along a beam,  
arms wide in the windy afternoon,  
and I heard, from some vanished natatorium,  
the brass band cough, the grandstand hush.

“He’ll attempt the forward three-and-a-half,  
a feat unseen since Stockholm—”

“He’s testing a joint,” you said,  
“with a hammer.”

The hammer rang. Below, the river  
opened its scoreless lanes.  
A truck crossed, rattling the century;  
pigeons burst like thrown bouquets.

Then the smallest inspector knelt  
and leaned his masked face toward a crack.

“Ah,” I whispered, “the veteran studies the water,  
calculating the cleanest entrance.”

“He’s measuring corrosion.”

“Ten points for concentration.”

“Zero points for listening.”

We walked beneath them, your hand  
firm at my elbow where the bank turned slick.  
Overhead, ropes hung down—  
towels, I claimed, for the contestants.

“Safety lines,” you said.

A wrench fell half an inch, caught,  
and swung above the current.

“The medal pendulum!”

“Tool lanyard.”

By dusk the inspectors climbed back,  
one after another, to solid pavement,  
no splash, no anthem, only traffic  
and the river keeping every secret.

You read the orange sign aloud:  
**STRUCTURAL SURVEY—DO NOT ENTER.**

I read instead the final standings,  
invented flags snapping in rain,  
the old divers bowing, silver-haired,  
to a crowd that remembered flight.

“They’re engineers,” you told me, softer now.

“Yes,” I said, as one looked down  
from the rail, helmet bright in the last sun.  
“But for a moment he was weightless.”

You considered the bridge, its burden,  
its rust mapped carefully against collapse.

“For a moment,” you allowed,  
“he did look very high up.”

And the river, practical as you,  
carried both our versions under.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a contemporary American poem set near the Tye River, contrasting an engineer’s literal view of a concrete span with the narrator’s imaginative vision of a diving board.
counterfactuals.output:
**Load-Bearing**

Near the Tye, where Route 56  
threads the Blue Ridge like a loose gray stitch,  
an engineer stops beneath the bridge  
and names what holds:

reinforced concrete,  
compression, shear,  
the measured fatigue of weather,  
the clean arithmetic of weight.

He taps a pier with his knuckles,  
listens for damage.  
Above us, trucks cross one by one,  
each tire briefly thunder.

But I look at the cantilevered deck  
reaching over green water  
and see a diving board—

the whole county waiting barefoot  
at its trembling end:  
orchards, mailboxes, rusted tractors,  
the Dollar General’s bright sign,

all of us taking one last breath  
before springing outward  
into whatever the river means  
when it flashes and refuses to answer.

The engineer says, *It doesn’t move.*

Still, a heron lifts from the shallows.  
Still, the mountain holds its breath.  
Still, in the heat, the bridge seems to bend—

not failing, exactly,  
but choosing  
the impossible blue below.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a bittersweet prose poem about two people driving across an aging bridge, ending with the ominous line “Our span is ready.”
counterfactuals.output:
The bridge shuddered beneath us, old iron remembering every winter. Rust feathered the railings; below, the river carried strips of sunset toward places we had once promised to go. You drove with both hands on the wheel, though there was no wind, and I watched your face flicker between the girders—light, shadow, light—like someone already becoming a memory.

Halfway across, we laughed about the first time: your broken radio, my shoes on the dashboard, the tollbooth keeper waving us through as if love were an emergency. Now the speakers breathed only static. Your shoulder leaned almost imperceptibly away from mine. Still, when the roadway groaned, our hands found each other above the console, faithful from habit or fear.

Ahead, warning lamps reddened the dusk. Behind us, the shore dwindled into a country we could no longer return to unchanged. The bridge gave another long, metallic sigh, and from somewhere beneath the river came a voice that sounded like both of us.

Our span is ready.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a poem that moves between dialogue, memory, and metaphor: a Stop/Slow road worker, three men on a bridge, imagined two-and-a-half gainers, and a relationship nearing its end.
counterfactuals.output:
At the county line a woman turns  
a paddle in her orange gloves.

**STOP**, it says,  
and the cars idle like held breath.

Behind her, three men lean on a bridge  
with their hard hats tipped toward the river.

“Deep enough?” one asks.

“For what?” says another.

The third only looks down,  
measuring the dark with his body.

You once told me you could do  
a two-and-a-half gainer from anywhere—  
quarry ledge, motel balcony,  
the last clean sentence of an argument.

I pictured you rising backward,  
knees gathered to your chest,  
the whole sky briefly yours,  
then water closing its blue fist.

But memory alters the height:  
we were younger; the bridge was summer;  
the river carried beer cans, cottonwood,  
everything we swore would float forever.

The worker turns the paddle.

**SLOW**, it says,  
which is not the same as stay.

One man spits over the rail.  
One says, “I’d never jump.”  
One spreads his arms just once—

not flying, not falling,  
only showing the air  
how wide a man can be.

In the car, you ask,  
“Are we almost through?”

Road tar shines in the heat.  
A flag snaps above the ditch.  
Between us, the silence attempts  
its own impossible dive:

two and a half turns  
from love into leaving,

no splash yet,  
no one looking away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
